lines.text: With an identiteitsbewijs (ID) you show who you are.
A proof of identity can be: a Dutch passport, a Dutch identity card, a passport from an EU country [EU-land], or a card [pasje] for foreigners [buitenlanders] who are in the Netherlands.
Sometimes you can also use your driving licence.
Everyone in the Netherlands aged fourteen and older must have a proof of identity and always carry it.
On public transport [openbaar vervoer (OV)] this already applies from age twelve.
Sometimes a child must have their own ID from birth: if you travel abroad or if the child needs medical care [medische zorg].
The police can ask for your proof of identity, for example if you get a fine/ticket [bekeuring].
An inspector [controleur] on public transport may also ask for it.
If you do not have it with you, you can get an extra fine.
The tasks of the police [taken van de politie]:
The police must protect [beschermen] people — come into action [actie] when people are in danger.
In an accident [ongeluk] where something must happen very quickly, you call the emergency number 112 [alarmnummer 112].
The police check whether everything follows the rules, for example in traffic.
Police officers can give a fine if someone does not follow the traffic rules [verkeersregels].
You must always do what the police say.

Filing a report with the police [Aangifte doen bij de politie]: if the situation is serious [ernstig], you are obliged [verplicht] to file a report — for example if someone has been murdered, or in case of rape [verkrachting].

In less serious situations you can also file a report or ask for help: in case of theft [diefstal] — your bike or phone was stolen, if you have lost something important (your passport), after an accident, in case of violence [geweld] — someone hit you, in case of fraud [fraude] or scamming [oplichting] — someone calls pretending to be from the bank, and in case of discrimination [discriminatie].
